report.source_text: A 72-year-old caucasian man suffering from angina pectoris, hypertension, type 2 diabetes, with a history of coronary angioplasty was admitted to the Department of Dermatology (Wroclaw Medical University, Poland) for diagnosis of a dark gray skin coloration which had been present for 4 months. The pigmentation intensity was most pronounced on the face, neck, and upper torso (Fig. 1). The patient reported general weakness, loss of appetite, weight loss, and dark urine for several weeks.

report.source_text: Four months later, a diagnostic skin biopsy was taken from his right shoulder area and revealed intracellular and extracellular melanin deposition in the dermis. Intracellular deposition of melanin was detected in two types of cells: CD68(+) macrophages and melanoma metastatic cells with immunohistochemical profile: Melan-A (+), HMB45 (+), S100(+), CD68 (−), distributed and grouped into deep layers of the dermis (Fig. 3).

clinician.trajectory_summary: A 72-year-old man with history of nodular malignant melanoma with sentinel node metastasis presented with a 4-month history of dark gray skin discoloration on face, neck, and upper torso, accompanied by systemic symptoms. Skin biopsy showed intracellular and extracellular melanin deposits in dermis with melanoma metastatic cells confirmed by positive Melan-A, HMB45, S100 immunostains. Imaging revealed a 2 cm renal tumor but no other macroscopic metastases. The extreme rarity of dermal melanosis in metastatic melanoma and lack of visible metastases delayed the diagnosis for four months.

Skin biopsy revealed intracellular and extracellular melanin deposition in dermis; melanoma metastatic cells were immunohistochemically positive for Melan-A, HMB45, and S100
Imaging showed a 2 cm tumor in right kidney but no widespread macroscopic metastases
Clinical course documented blue-gray skin discoloration appearing 9 months after second melanoma surgery
